text: The Beginner tier of this capstone built one thing: a tested customers mart, staged from the real jaffle shop raw_customers seed data. That mart works. It doesn't answer anything about revenue or order fulfillment — and now two different stakeholders want exactly that.

Finance's ask: a revenue number they trust, by day, by payment method, that doesn't move when they're not expecting it to. Ops's ask is a different shape from the same data: a count of orders in each status — placed, shipped, completed, returned — so they know where orders are piling up.

Both requests trace back to the same real source: raw_orders, one row per order, with a status column and a user_id tying back to the customers mart you already built. One well-built orders layer can serve both asks, instead of two one-off queries quietly drifting apart.

Here's the detail that matters for the rest of this chapter: raw_orders isn't a static seed file in this scenario. It gets new rows every day the shop is open. A model that re-reads the full history from scratch works fine today — it will not stay fine as that history grows. Keep that in mind.
Next lesson: planning the model layer — staging, intermediate, and marts for orders and payments, before any SQL gets written.
